newsitem.title: FRANCE: CYCLING-ROUS WINS WITH EASE AFTER 75-KM SOLO BREAK.
newsitem.headline: CYCLING-ROUS WINS WITH EASE AFTER 75-KM SOLO BREAK.

text.p: Frenchman Didier Rous broke away 75 kms from the finish to win the 18th stage of the Tour de France by more than five minutes on Thursday.
In a Festina team one-two, Rous was five minutes nine seconds ahead of compatriot Pascal Herve with American Bobby Julich third 5:10 behind in the 175.5-km stage from Colmar.
Rous, 26, benefitted from clever tactical support from his experienced Festina colleagues Laurent Dufaux of Switzerland and compatriot Herve.
The winner quoted Herve as saying "Off you go on your own" when the 33-year-old veteran saw victory was feasible.
Jan Ullrich of Germany retained the overall leader's yellow jersey after finishing in a large group 5:29 behind that also included Danish defending champion Bjarne Riis.
Rous had so much time that three kms from the finish he did some cheer-leading from the saddle as he sped towards the line.
Rous quoted his Festina leader Richard Virenque as saying before the start it was the last possible day for the team to achieve something.
"When we had a lead of 45 seconds I said perhaps we could turn the Tour upside down," Rous said and was given the go-ahead to attack.
"Ullrich looked in trouble, he's not in the best shape."
Rous said it was Festina's last chance to upset Ullrich's Telekom because they were not as strong as the German team in the sprints or Saturday's Disneyland time trial.
Festina, having won the previous day's stage through Australian Neil Stephens, attacked throughout the afternoon.

After about 80 kms, going into the climb of the 748-metre Hundsruck, a small group including Virenque, second overall, and third-placed Italian Marco Pantani attacked, opening as much as a 30-minute lead over the main peloton which included Ullrich.
Riis, who has been unwell for three days, fell some four minutes behind, but Ullrich hauled his way back and kept close to Virenque's tail.
"I'm really glad I was able to finish the stage today. I thought I wouldn't manage it," Riis said.

Rous went out alone on the last climb, reaching the top of the Ballon d'Alsace at 1,060 metres three minutes ahead of the chasing group and nearly five in front of the second group which contained Virenque and Ullrich.

Herve and Dufaux then helped Rous keep well ahead by riding side by side up to the summit, keeping the way blocked to the rest of the field with the cheering crowds lining both sides of the road barely one metre apart.
Rous was four minutes ahead of the first chasing group of nine men, including Herve and Dufaux, 40 kms from Montbeliard and six minutes in front of the main peloton.
The advantages increased to 4:20 and 7:10 with 25 kms to go.
Friday's relatively flat 172-km 19th stage to Dijon should see the sprinters come back to the fore.
